Uniform-Correct Policy Optimization: Breaking RLVR’s Indifference to Diversity

Anamika Lochab Affiliation: Department of Computer Science    Bolian Li Affiliation: Purdue University, West Lafayette    Ruqi Zhang Affiliation: {alochab, li4468, ruqiz}@purdue.edu
Abstract

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has achieved substantial gains in single-attempt accuracy (Pass@1) on reasoning tasks, yet often suffers from reduced multi-sample coverage (Pass@K), indicating diversity collapse. We identify a structural cause for this degradation: common RLVR objectives, such as GRPO, are indifferent to how probability mass is distributed among correct solutions. Combined with stochastic training dynamics, this indifference induces a self-reinforcing collapse, in which probability mass concentrates on a narrow subset of correct outputs while alternative valid solutions are suppressed. We formalize this collapse mechanism and further characterize the optimal policy structure under two complementary criteria: robustness and entropy-regularized optimality, which identify the Uniform-Correct Policy as uniquely optimal. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Uniform-Correct Policy Optimization (UCPO), a modification to GRPO that adds a conditional uniformity penalty on the policy’s distribution over correct solutions. The penalty redistributes gradient signal toward underrepresented correct responses, encouraging uniform allocation of probability mass within the correct set. Across three models (1.5B–7B parameters) and five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, UCPO improves Pass@K and diversity while maintaining competitive Pass@1, achieving up to +10% absolute improvement on AIME24 at Pass@64 and up to 45% higher equation-level diversity within the correct set.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving large language models (LLMs) on reasoning tasks such as mathematics and code generation, yielding substantial gains in single-attempt accuracy (Pass@1) across challenging reasoning benchmarks (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024; Karan and Du, 2025; Yue et al., 2025).

Despite these successes, RLVR often degrades Pass@K even as it improves Pass@1 (He et al., 2025; Cobbe et al., 2021; Song et al., 2025). This suggests that RL fine-tuning contracts the model’s solution space (Wu et al., 2026; Karan and Du, 2025), concentrating probability mass on a small subset of correct solutions while suppressing alternative valid reasoning paths present in the base model.

Most prior efforts address this issue (Wang et al., 2025b; He et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Cui et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025) through entropy bonuses, exploration incentives, or token-level constraints. While these methods can alleviate diversity loss, they share a common limitation: none directly specifies how probability mass should be distributed among correct solutions. Lacking a principled target, they rely on proxies that may satisfy local heuristics (e.g., token-level entropy) while the policy still concentrates mass on a few correct solutions.

In this work, we analyze RLVR from the perspective of optimal policy structure. We ask three questions: (i) what policies are optimal under standard RLVR objectives, and what policies are actually attained in practice; (ii) what policy should be considered optimal when multiple correct solutions exist; and (iii) how such a policy can be learned via RL. These questions guide our analysis and the design of a new RL objective.

We first show that the standard RLVR objective is fundamentally underspecified: it is indifferent to how probability mass is distributed among correct solutions. As a result, a fully collapsed policy and a maximally diverse policy will be considered equally optimal. Moreover, the stochastic dynamics of on-policy sampling induce a self-reinforcing collapse in which frequently sampled solutions are amplified by gradient updates and suppress alternatives. Thus, diversity collapse arises jointly from objective indifference and training dynamics.

We then study what the optimal policy should be when multiple correct solutions exist. We formalize this through two criteria: robustness optimality (which policy retains the best performance under distribution shift) and entropy-regularized optimality (which policy optimally balances correctness with diversity). Both identify the same solution: the Uniform-Correct Policy, which places zero mass on incorrect outputs while distributing probability uniformly across all correct solutions.

Motivated by this analysis, we propose Uniform-Correct Policy Optimization (UCPO), a simple modification of GRPO that admits the Uniform-Correct Policy as its unique optimum. UCPO adds a uniformity penalty over correct solutions, which redistributes gradient signal to amplify underrepresented solutions while tempering dominant ones.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We identify a fundamental limitation of RLVR: the objective is indifferent to how probability mass is distributed among correct solutions, allowing stochastic training dynamics to drive irreversible mode collapse. We validate this mechanism both theoretically (Section  4.2) and empirically through controlled experiments (Section  4.3).

  • •

    We theoretically characterize the optimal policy structure for RLVR through two criteria: robustness and entropy-regularized optimality (Section  5), proving that the Uniform-Correct Policy is optimal under both criteria.

  • •

    We derive Uniform-Correct Policy Optimization (UCPO) to achieve this optimal structure, and prove that the Uniform-Correct Policy is its unique optimum (Theorem  6.1). UCPO preserves the total advantage mass of GRPO but reallocates it toward underrepresented correct responses.

  • •

    Across three models (1.5B–7B parameters) and five mathematical benchmarks, UCPO consistently improves Pass@K and diversity while maintaining competitive Pass@1, achieving up to +10% absolute improvement on AIME24 at Pass@64 and up to 45% higher equation-level diversity within the correct set, with negligible training overhead.

2 Related Works

Prior works have documented diversity collapse in RLVR: fine-tuning improves Pass@1 but can reduce Pass@K by contracting the support of correct outputs and sharpening around high-likelihood base-model modes (Matsutani et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; He et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2025). A growing body of work aims to address this collapse, which we organize into analysis-driven methods that diagnose a collapse mechanism and derive a targeted fix, and methods that encourage diversity indirectly through token-level stochasticity or trajectory-level exploration.

2.1 Diagnosing and Addressing Diversity Collapse

Several concurrent works analyze mechanisms underlying diversity collapse and propose targeted interventions. Cui et al. (2025) attribute collapse to entropy decay driven by positive probability-advantage covariance, and propose covariance-based gradient clipping and KL regularization. Gai et al. (2025) show that selection and reinforcement biases in KL-regularized RLVR amplify base-policy imbalance within the correct set, and propose differential smoothing using sequence log-probabilities11 1 Their analysis is for KL-regularized RLVR, whereas our focus is on the RLVR objective itself. Throughout our analysis and experiments, we use β=0\beta=0, isolating collapse arising from the advantage-maximization term rather than reference regularization.. Plyusov et al. (2026) show that easy prompts with high success rates drive the strongest concentration of correctness mass, and propose focal advantage scaling to down-weight updates from these prompts. LAD (Li and Li, 2026) states that expected-advantage maximization distorts relative proportions among correct responses, and replaces it with an ff-divergence objective that preserves the previous policy’s proportions. By contrast, our work identifies that RLVR advantage-maximization objectives are indifferent to within-correct set allocation. The proposed UCPO reshapes the within-correct distribution toward uniformity by redistributing gradient mass among correct responses.

2.2 Diversity via Token-Level Regularization and Trajectory-Level Exploration

Entropy-based methods aim to mitigate collapse by maintaining stochasticity during training. Global entropy regularization acts over the full output space, which can increase probability mass on incorrect responses and conflict with correctness. More targeted token-level methods preserve local stochasticity through entropy bonuses, high-uncertainty token updates, or selective entropy regularization (Cheng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Jiang et al., 2025). However, a model can remain uncertain at the token-level while still collapsing to a narrow set of final solutions (Wu et al., 2026). Another line of work promotes diversity by broadening trajectory-level exploration through adaptive rollout allocation, targeted exploration, or external data (Liao et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025). These methods are complementary to UCPO as they expand the set of reasoning trajectories explored during training, while UCPO operates at the conditional-distribution level, reshaping how gradient mass is allocated among correct responses once they are sampled.

3 Preliminaries

We review the Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) setting and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

3.1 RLVR Objective

Let xx denote a prompt and yy a model completion sampled from a policy πθ​(y∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x). In RLVR, correctness is determined by a verifier R⁡(x,y)∈{0,1}R(x,y)\in\{0,1\}, and the set of verifier-accepted (correct) solutions is

𝒴+​(x)={y:R⁡(x,y)=1}.\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)=\{y:R(x,y)=1\}.

The RLVR objective maximizes the probability of producing any correct solution:

J(πθ)=𝔼x∼𝒟𝔼y∼πθ(⋅|x)[R(x,y)]=𝔼x∼𝒟[∑y∈𝒴+​(x)πθ(y|x)].\begin{aligned} J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[R(x,y)]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\right]\end{aligned}. (1)

We denote the total probability mass the policy places on correct outputs as

Zθ​(x)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)πθ​(y∣x),Z_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x), (2)

so that J⁡(πθ)=𝔼x∼𝒟​[Zθ​(x)]J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[Z_{\theta}(x)]. Maximizing the RLVR objective is therefore equivalent to maximizing Zθ​(x)Z_{\theta}(x), or equivalently log⁡Zθ​(x)\log Z_{\theta}(x). Taking the gradient of Eq. (1) yields the standard policy gradient form:

∇θJ(πθ)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[R(x,y)∇θlogπθ(y∣x)].\nabla_{\theta}J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\;y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[R(x,y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right]. (3)

The gradient signal depends only on whether yy is correct, not on how probability mass is distributed among different correct outputs.

3.2 Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)

GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) estimates RLVR policy gradients using group-relative baselines. For each prompt xx, it samples KK rollouts {yi}i=1K∼πold(⋅∣x)\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(\cdot\mid x) from the rollout policy, obtains rewards Ri=R⁡(x,yi)R_{i}=R(x,y_{i}), and updates the current policy πθ\pi_{\theta} using importance ratios. Let σR=std⁡({Rj}j=1K)\sigma_{R}=\operatorname{std}(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{K}) denote the within-group reward standard deviation. The group-relative baseline and advantage are

R¯=1K​∑i=1KRi,Ai=Ri−R¯σR+ε.\bar{R}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}R_{i},\quad\quad A_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\bar{R}}{\sigma_{R}+\varepsilon}. (4)

Following PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), GRPO uses the clipped surrogate objective:

LGRPO​(θ)\displaystyle L_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta) =𝔼x∼𝒟,{yi}i=1K∼πold(⋅∣x)[∑i=1Kmin(ri(θ)Ai,clip(ri(θ),1−ε,1+ε)Ai)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}\sim\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot\mid x)}\Bigg[\sum_{i=1}^{K}\min\Big(r_{i}(\theta)A_{i},\mathrm{clip}\!\left(r_{i}(\theta),1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon\right)A_{i}\Big)\Bigg] (5)

where ri​(θ)=πθ​(yi|x)πold​(yi|x)r_{i}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i}|x)} is the importance ratio. All correct responses share advantage A+A^{+}, and all incorrect responses share A−.A^{-}. Consequently, GRPO inherits the RLVR objective’s indifference to how probability mass is allocated within the correct set.

4 Structural Causes of Diversity Collapse in RLVR

We identify a structural limitation of RLVR objectives: they are indifferent to how probability mass is distributed among correct solutions. Combined with optimization dynamics, this indifference leads to systematic diversity collapse.

4.1 Objective Indifference

The RLVR objective (Eq. (1)) specifies what the policy should produce (correct outputs) but not how probability mass should be distributed among multiple correct solutions. The following theorem formalizes this observation.

Theorem 4.1 (Stationary Points of RLVR).

Let π\pi be any policy such that supp(π(⋅∣x))⊆𝒴+(x)\operatorname{supp}(\pi(\cdot\mid x))\subseteq\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x), i.e., π\pi places all probability mass on correct outputs. Then π\pi is a stationary point of the RLVR objective (Eq. (1)).

Proof.

The RLVR objective is J⁡(π)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)π⁡(y∣x).J(\pi)\;=\;\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y^{+}}(x)}\pi(y\mid x). For any policy with supp(π(⋅∣x))⊆𝒴+(x)\operatorname{supp}(\pi(\cdot\mid x))\subseteq\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x), we have J⁡(π)=1J(\pi)=1, the maximum possible value. Since JJ is linear in π\pi and the constraint set

{π|∑yπ(y∣x)=1,π(y∣x)≥0}\left\{\pi\;\middle|\;\sum_{y}\pi(y\mid x)=1,\;\pi(y\mid x)\geq 0\right\}

is a simplex, any policy achieving J⁡(π)=1J(\pi)=1 is a global maximizer of the RLVR objective. ∎

Remark 4.1 (Implication of Theorem  4.1).

Theorem  4.1 implies that the following policies are all stationary points of RLVR with identical objective value J⁡(π)=1J(\pi)=1:

  • •

    Collapsed: π⁡(y1∣x)=1\pi(y_{1}\mid x)=1 for some y1∈𝒴+​(x)y_{1}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x), and π⁡(y∣x)=0\pi(y\mid x)=0 otherwise.

  • •

    Uniform-correct: π⁡(y∣x)=1|𝒴+​(x)|\pi(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|} for all y∈𝒴+​(x)y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x).

  • •

    Any mixture: Any distribution supported exclusively on 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x).

Thus, the RLVR objective (and by extension GRPO and other variants) provides no gradient signal to distinguish among these policies once all mass is on correct outputs. The choice among stationary points is determined entirely by optimization dynamics, not by the objective itself.

4.2 The Collapse Mechanism

Section 4.1 established that RLVR objectives do not specify how probability mass should be allocated among correct responses. We now show that, under GRPO and related group-relative policy-gradient methods, on-policy sampling resolves this ambiguity by favoring concentration: sampling imbalances are amplified across updates, concentrating mass on a subset of correct responses. We formalize this as a four-step cycle and validate each step in controlled experiments where the full policy distribution is observable (Appendix B); proofs are provided in Appendix A.1.

4.2.1 Setup

Consider training a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} initialized from πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. For a prompt xx, let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be the finite output space, partitioned into correct responses 𝒴+={y1,…,ym}\mathcal{Y}^{+}=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\} and incorrect responses 𝒴−\mathcal{Y}^{-}. Under GRPO, all correct responses share advantage A+A^{+} and all incorrect responses share A−A^{-}. Throughout this section, yiy_{i} denotes a cluster of solutions sharing the same underlying reasoning strategy.

4.2.2 Sampling Bias

The GRPO objective involves an expectation over the policy:

ℒ(θ)=𝔼y∼πθ(⋅|x)[A(y)⋅logπθ(y|x)].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[A(y)\cdot\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\right]. (6)

Since this expectation is intractable, GRPO approximates it via Monte Carlo: drawing KK i.i.d. rollouts from πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x) and computing the empirical gradient. Let NyN_{y} denote the number of samples from solution yy among the KK rollouts.

Proposition 4.1 (Sampling Bias).

Under on-policy sampling, solutions with higher probability are sampled more frequently. For KK i.i.d. rollouts from πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x), the sample count NyN_{y} follows:

Ny∼Binomial⁡(K,πθ​(y|x)),𝔼⁡[Ny]=K⋅πθ​(y|x).N_{y}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(K,\pi_{\theta}(y|x)),\quad\mathbb{E}[N_{y}]=K\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y|x). (7)
Proof.

Each rollout independently produces solution yy with probability πθ​(y|x)\pi_{\theta}(y|x). The count of successes in KK independent Bernoulli trials is binomial. ∎

Higher-probability solutions are therefore overrepresented in sampled batches. Even under a uniform policy, finite-batch multinomial sampling can produce unequal counts across correct responses; Proposition A.1 formalizes this sampling-induced symmetry breaking. Appendix B.2 empirically validates this effect in the controlled environment: under uniform initialization, GRPO amplifies whichever correct response is overrepresented, leading to collapse to an arbitrary winner. The key question is therefore whether the subsequent gradient step corrects this imbalance or amplifies it.

4.2.3 Gradient Amplification

Since sampling produces unequal counts {Ny}\{N_{y}\}, we now examine how this imbalance enters the gradient update. The GRPO gradient over the batch is:

∇θℒ=∑i=1KAi⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(yi|x).\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}=\sum_{i=1}^{K}A_{i}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x). (8)

Grouping by solution, the gradient contribution of each correct y∈𝒴+y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+} is: Ny⋅A+⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(y|x).N_{y}\cdot A^{+}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x).

Theorem 4.2 (Gradient Amplification).

Under GRPO with on-policy sampling, the expected gradient contribution from a correct solution y∈𝒴+y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+} is:

𝔼[∑i:yi=yA+∇θlogπθ(y|x)]=A+⋅K⋅πθ(y|x)⋅∇θlogπθ(y|x).\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i:y_{i}=y}A^{+}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\right]=A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x). (9)

Thus, expected gradient contribution scales with current probability: high-probability solutions receive larger updates, while solutions with πθ​(y∣x)≪1/K\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\ll 1/K are likely unsampled and lose mass through softmax renormalization.

4.2.4 Divergence of Probability Ratios

The combination of sampling bias and gradient amplification causes probability ratios to diverge over training.

Theorem 4.3 (Compounding Divergence).

Let πt\pi_{t} denote the policy after tt updates. Under GRPO, for two correct solutions y1,y2∈𝒴+​(x)y_{1},y_{2}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x) with π0​(y1|x)>π0​(y2|x)\pi_{0}(y_{1}|x)>\pi_{0}(y_{2}|x), the expected change in their log-probability ratio at step tt is:

𝔼⁡[Δ​log⁡πt​(y1|x)πt​(y2|x)]=η⋅A+⋅K⋅(πt​(y1|x)−πt​(y2|x))>0,\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\log\frac{\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)}{\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x)}\right]=\eta\cdot A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\bigl(\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)-\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x)\bigr)>0, (10)

where η\eta is the effective learning rate. The log-ratio is a submartingale with positive drift that increases as the probability gap widens.

This feedback causes small initial asymmetries to compound: the dominant solution receives larger updates, increasing its probability and expected sample count in subsequent batches, widening the gap and reinforcing the collapse.

4.2.5 Irreversible Pruning

The collapse becomes irreversible once minority solutions fall below the sampling threshold.

Corollary 4.1 (Sampling Threshold).

When πt​(y|x)≪1/K\pi_{t}(y|x)\ll 1/K, the probability that solution yy receives at least one sample in a batch of size KK is:

P⁡(Ny≥1)=1−(1−πt​(y|x))K≈K⋅πt​(y|x)≪1.P(N_{y}\geq 1)=1-(1-\pi_{t}(y|x))^{K}\approx K\cdot\pi_{t}(y|x)\ll 1.

Below this threshold, solution yy receives effectively zero gradient signal and cannot recover under on-policy sampling.

The four steps trace a complete trajectory: (i) initial asymmetries arise from sampling bias, (ii) GRPO amplifies these asymmetries into the gradient, (iii) the updated policy increases the probability gap, which worsens sampling imbalance in subsequent iterations, and (iv) once low-probability solutions fall below the sampling threshold, recovery becomes unlikely. This mechanism explains the empirical Pass@1 versus Pass@KK trade-off( Figure 9): GRPO improves single-sample accuracy while reducing multi-sample coverage.

4.3 Controlled Experiment

To validate the proposed collapse mechanism, we construct a controlled RLVR environment with a softmax policy over a finite discrete output space, of which three outputs are correct and the remainder are incorrect. This makes the full policy distribution exactly observable throughout training (details in Appendix B). Figure 1 confirms all four stages of the collapse cycle; for details see Appendix B.1.

5 The Optimal Policy

We established that GRPO induces systematic collapse toward dominant correct solutions, we now ask: what should the optimal policy look like when multiple correct solutions exist? We formalize this question through the conditional distribution over correct outputs and prove that a specific structure, uniform probability across all correct solutions, is optimal under two independent criteria.

5.1 Conditional Distribution on Correct Outputs

Here Z⁡(x)Z(x) is the total probability that the policy produces a correct answer. While RLVR optimizes Z⁡(x)Z(x), it leaves the structure of q⁡(y∣x)q(y\mid x) unconstrained. Diversity collapse corresponds to qq concentrating on a small subset of 𝒴+\mathcal{Y^{+}}.

5.2 The Uniform-Correct Policy

This policy places all probability mass on correct outputs and distributes it uniformly among them. We show that this structure is optimal under two complementary criteria: Robustness under distribution shift, which guards against test-time conditions that differ from training, and Entropy-regularized Optimality, a standard theoretical principle for resolving reward indifference (proofs in Appendix A.3).

Theorem 5.1 (Robustness under distribution shift).

Suppose a distribution shift disables a subset S⊂𝒴+S\subset\mathcal{Y^{+}} of correct outputs, where |S|≤s|S|\leq s. Consider the robust objective:

maxπminS:|S|≤s∑y∈𝒴+∖Sπ(y|x).\max_{\pi}\min_{S:|S|\leq s}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y^{+}}\setminus S}\pi(y|x). (12)

Then the Uniform-Correct Policy uniquely maximizes the worst-case retained probability mass.

Theorem 5.2.

Consider the entropy-regularized objective

maxπ(⋅∣x)𝔼y∼π[R(x,y)]+τH(π(⋅∣x)).\max_{\pi(\cdot\mid x)}\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[R(x,y)]+\tau\,\mathrm{H}(\pi(\cdot\mid x)). (13)

There exists a threshold τ0>0\tau_{0}>0 such that for all 0<τ<τ00<\tau<\tau_{0}, the UCP uniquely maximizes Eq. (13).

Theorem 5.1 establishes that the Uniform-Correct Policy is the minimax-optimal solution against the loss of any bounded subset of correct outputs, and Theorem 5.2 shows that it is the unique solution to the entropy-regularized objective for sufficiently small τ\tau.

6 UCPO: Uniform Correct Policy Optimization

Section 5 established that the uniform-correct policy is uniquely optimal. We now derive an objective that targets this policy during training.

6.1 UCPO Motivation

A direct way to operationalize Theorem 5.2 is global entropy regularization. However, the optimization dynamics of this approach hinder convergence to the UCP. Because global entropy acts over the full output space, it can increase mass on incorrect outputs rather than controlling the conditional distribution over correct responses. Empirically, it yields small and less consistent Pass@K gains and is sensitive to the entropy coefficient; see Appendix C for details.

This motivates an objective that directly controls how the policy allocates mass among correct responses. We therefore propose Uniform-Correct Policy Optimization (UCPO), which augments correctness-mass maximization with a conditional uniformity penalty that encourages the policy to match the uniform distribution over correct responses. UCPO therefore increases total correctness mass while promoting a balanced allocation of probability mass within the correct set.

6.2 Objective

For a prompt x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}, let 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x) be the set of correct responses. During training, we sample NN rollouts from πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x). The correct rollouts y∈𝒴+​(x)y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x) are effectively samples from the conditional policy qθ(⋅|x)q_{\theta}(\cdot|x):

qθ​(y∣x)=πθ​(y∣x)Zθ​(x),Zθ​(x)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)πθ​(y∣x)q_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{Z_{\theta}(x)},\qquad Z_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)

where Zθ​(x)Z_{\theta}(x) is the total probability mass that the model places on all the correct responses. We also define the uniform distribution over the correct set:

u⁡(y∣x)=1|𝒴+​(x)|.u(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|}.

We propose the Uniform-Correct Policy Optimization (UCPO) objective:

LUCPO​(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟​[log⁡Zθ​(x)⏟correctness mass−τ​KL(u(⋅∣x)∥qθ(⋅∣x)⏟uniformity penalty]L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\underbrace{\log Z_{\theta}(x)}_{\text{correctness mass}}-\tau\,\underbrace{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.9023}\mathrm{KL}(u(\cdot\mid x)\|q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}}_{\text{uniformity penalty}}\right] (14)

Relative to GRPO, UCPO introduces a single additional term: the conditional uniformity penalty KL(u∥qθ)\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}). At τ=0\tau=0, UCPO reduces to GRPO. For τ>0\tau>0, the added term breaks GRPO’s indifference to within-correct mass allocation and biases the policy toward the uniform-correct target. In particular, the Uniform-Correct Policy is the unique optimum of the UCPO objective (Theorem 6.1). This modification incurs negligible additional computational overhead, since the penalty can be estimated from the same verifier-accepted rollouts already used by GRPO. As τ\tau increases, the penalty increasingly discourages concentration, pushing qθq_{\theta} toward the uniform target established in Section 5.

Theorem 6.1 (Uniform-correct policy is the unique optimum of UCPO).

Fix a prompt xx and consider the UCPO objective:

LUCPO(x)=logZθ(x)−τKL(u(⋅∣x)∥qθ(⋅∣x)).L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x)=\log Z_{\theta}(x)-\tau\,\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(u(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr).

For any τ>0\tau>0, the unique maximizer of LUCPO​(x)L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x) over policies πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) is the Uniform-Correct Policy.

6.3 Gradient Estimation

UCPO counteracts collapse through its gradient structure. Although GRPO is indifferent to within-correct allocation at the objective level, its sampled update effectively weights correct responses according to the current conditional distribution qθq_{\theta}. UCPO instead interpolates between qθq_{\theta} and the uniform target, shifting gradient mass away from dominant correct solutions and toward underrepresented ones.

Proposition 6.1 (Gradient Decomposition).

For any prompt xx with 𝒴+​(x)≠∅\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)\neq\emptyset,

∇θLUCPO​(x)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)[(1−τ)​qθ​(y∣x)+τ​u​(y∣x)]​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y∣x).\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\Big[(1-\tau)\,q_{\theta}(y\mid x)+\tau\,u(y\mid x)\Big]\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x). (15)

The proof is provided in Appendix A.4. The first term is estimated directly from the nn correct rollouts. The second term requires samples from the uniform distribution uu, which we estimate via importance sampling. Since u⁡(y)/qθ​(y)∝1/qθ​(y)u(y)/q_{\theta}(y)\propto 1/q_{\theta}(y), we define inverse weights vi=1/q^iv_{i}=1/\hat{q}_{i}, where

q^i=πθ​(yi∣x)∑j=1nπθ​(yj∣x),\hat{q}_{i}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\pi_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid x)},

with the derivation given in Appendix A.5. The resulting estimator is

∇θLUCPO≈∑i=1nwi​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣x),wi=1−τn+τ⋅vi∑j=1nvj.\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}\approx\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x),\qquad w_{i}=\frac{1-\tau}{n}+\tau\cdot\frac{v_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}}.

By construction, ∑iwi=1\sum_{i}w_{i}=1. Consequently, low-probability correct solutions receive larger weights, directly counteracting the sampling bias identified in Section 4.2.

Equivalently, UCPO redistributes GRPO’s total advantage budget n⋅A+n\cdot A^{+} according to wiw_{i}, giving larger updates to underrepresented correct solutions:

AiUCPO=n⋅A+⋅wi.A_{i}^{\mathrm{UCPO}}=n\cdot A^{+}\cdot w_{i}. (16)
Proposition 6.2 (Mass Preservation).

∑i=1nAiUCPO=∑i=1nAiGRPO\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{\mathrm{UCPO}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}.

Thus, UCPO preserves the total advantage mass assigned to correct rollouts and reallocates it towards underrepresented correct responses. The proof is provided in Appendix A.6.

7 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate UCPO across multiple model families, parameter scales, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

7.1 Setup

We train on 10K competition-style math problems from the DeepScaleR corpus (Luo et al., 2025; Liao et al., 2025), with 500 reserved for validation. We evaluate on three models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), and Qwen2.5-7B (Team, 2024). All models are fine-tuned from public checkpoints using the same RLVR pipeline.

We compare UCPO against standard GRPO and five diversity-preserving baselines with varying strategies for mitigating collapse in RLVR: adding entropy to the objective (Ent-Reg), adding an entropy-based advantage bonus (Ent-Adv) (Cheng et al., 2025), applying covariance-based KL control (KL-Cov) (Cui et al., 2025), optimizing a Pass@K-oriented reward with analytical advantages (Pass@K Training) (Chen et al., 2025), and using focal-style prompt-level advantage scaling (FGRPO). Dataset composition and implementation details are in Appendix D.

We evaluate on AIME 2024/2025 (Li et al., 2024), AMC 2023 (Li et al., 2024), MATH 500 (Gao et al., 2024), and OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024), reporting Pass@1 and Pass@K (K=64). Pass@K captures coverage over distinct correct solutions, making it suitable for evaluating diversity.

7.2 Main Results

Table 1 reports Pass@1 and Pass@64 across 5 benchmarks and 3 models (1.5B to 7B parameters). Across all settings, GRPO improves Pass@1 but saturates at larger KK, indicating concentration of probability mass on a small subset of correct solutions. UCPO maintains competitive Pass@1 while achieving consistent improvements at larger KK.

On DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, UCPO improves average Pass@64 to 78.27%, outperforming GRPO by +3.5 points while remaining comparable at Pass@1. Gains are particularly strong on AIME25 (+6.7) and AMC (+6.0) at K=64K{=}64. On DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B, UCPO improves average Pass@64 by +3.6 points, with +10.0 on AIME24. On Qwen2.5-7B, UCPO achieves the highest average Pass@64 (73.19%, +4.8 over GRPO) while also maintaining the strong Pass@1. These gains indicate that UCPO improves coverage over correct solutions rather than trading off accuracy for diversity.

7.3 Diversity

To directly measure diversity within the correct set, we evaluate equation-level diversity among verifier-accepted solutions (Table 2). This metric computes the fraction of mathematical expressions in a correct rollout that are unique relative to other correct rollouts for the same prompt (Hu et al., 2025). Higher values indicate more distinct reasoning trajectories.

UCPO consistently achieves the highest diversity across all benchmarks, with substantial improvements over GRPO (e.g., +45% on AIME, +13% on MATH). In contrast, entropy-based methods do not reliably improve diversity within the correct set and in some cases reduce it. This confirms that UCPO’s Pass@K gains arise from recovering distinct correct reasoning trajectories, not from spreading mass indiscriminately. This is consistent with the controlled experiments in Appendix B: GRPO collapses the conditional distribution over correct solutions, while UCPO maintains a more uniform allocation.

7.4 Pass@K Performance

Figures 7 show Pass@K curves for all three models and reasoning benchmarks. UCPO consistently improves performance at larger KK while remaining competitive at Pass@1, particularly on challenging benchmarks (AIME 2024/2025). This shows UCPO increases coverage over correct reasoning trajectories rather than concentrating on a single dominant mode. By redistributing gradient signal within the verifier-accepted set, UCPO prevents a small number of high-probability solutions from dominating learning, yielding sustained Pass@K gains without shifting mass toward incorrect outputs.

7.5 Cost and Hyperparameter Sensitivity

UCPO introduces a single hyperparameter τ\tau beyond standard GRPO. Its training cost is effectively identical to GRPO (Appendix E.2). UCPO is also robust across a moderate range of τ\tau values, whereas global entropy regularization is more sensitive to its coefficient (Appendix E.3).

8 Conclusion

We identify a structural limitation of RLVR training: while it increases the probability of correct solutions, it is indifferent to how probability mass is distributed within the correct set. This indifference, coupled with on-policy sampling dynamics, leads to diversity collapse and degraded multi-sample coverage (Pass@K). We show that the optimal policy is the Uniform-Correct Policy, which distributes probability evenly across correct solutions. To achieve this structure, we proposed UCPO, to reweight gradients conditional on correctness, amplifying underrepresented correct solutions while tempering dominant ones. Across multiple models and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, UCPO consistently improves Pass@K while preserving Pass@1, achieving up to a 10% absolute gain on AIME24 at Pass@64. These results highlight the importance of explicitly shaping the diversity structure of policies in RL for LLMs.
