Appendix A Theoretical Details and Proofs

A.1 The Diversity Collapse Mechanism

Sampling Bias: Connection to Pólya Urn and Preferential Attachment

The sampling bias in the collapse mechanism is mathematically related to classical models of preferential attachment: Consider Pólya Urn Analogy of an urn containing balls of MM colors (representing MM correct solutions), with initial counts proportional to {π0​(yi)}\{\pi_{0}(y_{i})\}. At each step, draw KK balls with replacement, observe their colors, then add balls proportionally to the observed counts. This is the Pólya urn process, known to converge to a random limit where one color dominates with positive probability.

GRPO’s on-policy sampling implements an analogous dynamic: the “urn composition” (policy distribution) is updated proportionally to observed samples (gradient updates), creating identical rich-get-richer dynamics.

Unequal sample counts are inevitable

Whether or not the policy initially assigns equal probability to correct solutions, the sample counts {Ny}y∈𝒴+\{N_{y}\}_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}} will be unequal:

  • •

    Deterministic case: If π⁡(y1|x)>π⁡(y2|x)\pi(y_{1}|x)>\pi(y_{2}|x), then 𝔼⁡[Ny1]>𝔼⁡[Ny2]\mathbb{E}[N_{y_{1}}]>\mathbb{E}[N_{y_{2}}]. Higher-probability solutions are systematically over-represented.

  • •

    Stochastic case: Even if π⁡(y|x)=1/m\pi(y|x)=1/m for all y∈𝒴+y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}, the realized counts will differ due to sampling variance (see Proposition A.1 and empirical illustration in Appendix  B).

Proposition A.1 (Stochastic Symmetry Breaking).

Suppose π0​(y|x)=1/m\pi_{0}(y|x)=1/m for all y∈𝒴+​(x)y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x). For any finite batch size KK, with positive probability, the sample counts {Ny}\{N_{y}\} are not all equal.

Proof.

Under a uniform policy over the mm correct responses, the count vector satisfies

(Ny1,…,Nym)∼Multinomial⁡(K,(1m,…,1m)).(N_{y_{1}},\ldots,N_{y_{m}})\sim\mathrm{Multinomial}\!\left(K,\left(\frac{1}{m},\ldots,\frac{1}{m}\right)\right).

If KK is not divisible by mm, exact equality of all counts is impossible. If KK is divisible by mm, exact equality requires Nyj=K/mN_{y_{j}}=K/m for every jj, which occurs with probability

ℙ⁡(Ny1=⋯=Nym=K/m)=K!((K/m)!)m⋅1mK<1.\mathbb{P}(N_{y_{1}}=\cdots=N_{y_{m}}=K/m)=\frac{K!}{((K/m)!)^{m}}\cdot\frac{1}{m^{K}}<1.

Thus, unequal counts occur with positive probability in any finite batch. On this event, at least one correct response is overrepresented, i.e., there exists y∗y^{*} such that Ny∗>K/mN_{y^{*}}>K/m. Across repeated independent batches, the probability that no imbalance ever occurs is zero, so symmetry-breaking occurs almost surely over training. ∎

A.2 Proof of Theorem  4.2, Theorem  4.3 and Corollary 4.1

Theorem A.1 (Gradient Amplification).

Under GRPO with on-policy sampling, the expected gradient contribution from a correct solution y∈𝒴+y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+} is:

𝔼[∑i:yi=yA+∇θlogπθ(y|x)]=A+⋅K⋅πθ(y|x)⋅∇θlogπθ(y|x).\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i:y_{i}=y}A^{+}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\right]=A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x). (17)

The expected contribution is proportional to current probability π⁡(y|x)\pi(y|x). Solutions with higher probability receive larger expected updates; solutions with π⁡(y|x)≪1/K\pi(y|x)\ll 1/K likely remain unsampled and receive no gradient signal, causing their probability to decrease through softmax renormalization.

Proof.

The GRPO gradient aggregated over the batch is:

∇θℒ=∑i=1KAi⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(yi|x).\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}=\sum_{i=1}^{K}A_{i}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x).

For correct solutions (yi∈𝒴+y_{i}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}), the advantage is Ai=A+A_{i}=A^{+}. Grouping terms by solution identity:

∇θℒ|𝒴+=∑y∈𝒴+Ny⋅A+⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(y|x),\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}\big|_{\mathcal{Y}^{+}}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}N_{y}\cdot A^{+}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x),

where Ny=∑i=1K𝟏[yi=y]N_{y}=\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}[y_{i}=y] counts occurrences of yy in the batch.

Taking expectations and applying Proposition 4.1:

𝔼⁡[Ny⋅A+⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(y|x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[N_{y}\cdot A^{+}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\right] =A+⋅𝔼⁡[Ny]⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(y|x)\displaystyle=A^{+}\cdot\mathbb{E}[N_{y}]\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x) (18)
=A+⋅K⋅πθ​(y|x)⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(y|x).\displaystyle=A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x). (19)

The expected gradient contribution is proportional to πθ​(y|x)\pi_{\theta}(y|x):

  • •

    High-probability solutions: πθ​(y|x)\pi_{\theta}(y|x) large ⇒\Rightarrow large expected contribution

  • •

    Low-probability solutions: πθ​(y|x)\pi_{\theta}(y|x) small ⇒\Rightarrow small expected contribution

  • •

    Very low probability (πθ​(y|x)≪1/K\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\ll 1/K): 𝔼⁡[Ny]≪1\mathbb{E}[N_{y}]\ll 1, so yy is likely unsampled and contributes nothing

For an unsampled solution yunsampy_{\text{unsamp}}:

Δ​zyunsamp=0(no gradient signal)\Delta z_{y_{\text{unsamp}}}=0\quad\text{(no gradient signal)} (20)

After the update, the softmax normalization means:

πθ′​(yunsamp|x)=exp⁡(zyunsamp)∑y′exp⁡(zy′+Δ​zy′)<πθ​(yunsamp|x)\pi^{\prime}_{\theta}(y_{\text{unsamp}}|x)=\frac{\exp(z_{y_{\text{unsamp}}})}{\sum_{y^{\prime}}\exp(z_{y^{\prime}}+\Delta z_{y^{\prime}})}<\pi_{\theta}(y_{\text{unsamp}}|x) (21)

The unsampled solution’s probability decreases as the probability mass shifts toward solutions that were sampled. This creates a multiplicative dynamic: solutions that are already more probable receive larger updates because they are more probable and sampled more often. After each gradient step, the probability distribution over 𝒴+\mathcal{Y}^{+} becomes more concentrated: the gap between high- and low-probability correct solutions widens. Since ∇θ​log​πθ​(y|x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x) points in the direction that increases πθ​(y|x)\pi_{\theta}(y|x), solutions with higher current probability receive updates of larger expected magnitude, amplifying the initial disparity. ∎

Theorem A.2 (Compounding Divergence).

Let πt\pi_{t} denote the policy after tt updates. Under GRPO, for two correct solutions y1,y2∈𝒴+​(x)y_{1},y_{2}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x) with π0​(y1|x)>π0​(y2|x)\pi_{0}(y_{1}|x)>\pi_{0}(y_{2}|x), the expected change in their log-probability ratio at step tt is:

𝔼⁡[Δ​log⁡πt​(y1|x)πt​(y2|x)]=η⋅A+⋅K⋅(πt​(y1|x)−πt​(y2|x))>0,\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\log\frac{\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)}{\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x)}\right]=\eta\cdot A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\bigl(\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)-\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x)\bigr)>0, (22)

where η\eta is the effective learning rate. The log-ratio is a submartingale with positive drift that increases as the probability gap widens.

Proof.

Under softmax parameterization, πt​(y|x)=exp⁡(zy)/Z\pi_{t}(y|x)=\exp(z_{y})/Z where Z=∑y′exp⁡(zy′)Z=\sum_{y^{\prime}}\exp(z_{y^{\prime}}). The log-probability ratio is:

log⁡πt​(y1|x)πt​(y2|x)=zy1−zy2.\log\frac{\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)}{\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x)}=z_{y_{1}}-z_{y_{2}}.

From Theorem 4.2, the expected logit update is:

𝔼⁡[Δ​zy]=η⋅A+⋅K⋅πt​(y|x),\mathbb{E}[\Delta z_{y}]=\eta\cdot A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\pi_{t}(y|x),

where η\eta absorbs learning rate and gradient-to-logit conversion factors.

The expected change in the log-ratio is:

𝔼⁡[Δ​log⁡πt​(y1|x)πt​(y2|x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\log\frac{\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)}{\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x)}\right] =𝔼⁡[Δ​zy1]−𝔼⁡[Δ​zy2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Delta z_{y_{1}}]-\mathbb{E}[\Delta z_{y_{2}}] (23)
=η⋅A+⋅K⋅πt​(y1|x)−η⋅A+⋅K⋅πt​(y2|x)\displaystyle=\eta\cdot A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)-\eta\cdot A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x) (24)
=η⋅A+⋅K⋅(πt​(y1|x)−πt​(y2|x)).\displaystyle=\eta\cdot A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\bigl(\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)-\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x)\bigr). (25)

When πt​(y1|x)>πt​(y2|x)\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)>\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x), this quantity is strictly positive. Moreover, as training progresses:

  • •

    πt​(y1|x)\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x) increases (receiving larger updates)

  • •

    πt​(y2|x)\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x) decreases (receiving smaller updates, or losing mass to normalization)

  • •

    The gap πt​(y1|x)−πt​(y2|x)\pi_{t}(y_{1}|x)-\pi_{t}(y_{2}|x) widens

  • •

    The drift in (22) increases

This establishes that the log-ratio diverges with accelerating speed: the collapse is not merely linear but compounds over training. ∎

Corollary A.1 (Sampling Threshold).

When πt​(y|x)≪1/K\pi_{t}(y|x)\ll 1/K, the probability that solution yy receives at least one sample in a batch of size KK is:

P⁡(Ny≥1)=1−(1−πt​(y|x))K≈K⋅πt​(y|x)≪1P(N_{y}\geq 1)=1-(1-\pi_{t}(y|x))^{K}\approx K\cdot\pi_{t}(y|x)\ll 1

Below this threshold, solution yy receives effectively zero gradient signal and cannot recover under on-policy sampling.

Proof.

The probability that yy is never sampled in KK trials is:

P⁡(Ny=0)=(1−πt​(y|x))KP(N_{y}=0)=(1-\pi_{t}(y|x))^{K}

Thus:

P⁡(Ny≥1)=1−(1−πt​(y|x))KP(N_{y}\geq 1)=1-(1-\pi_{t}(y|x))^{K}

For small πt​(y|x)\pi_{t}(y|x), using (1−p)K≈e−K​p≈1−K​p(1-p)^{K}\approx e^{-Kp}\approx 1-Kp for K​p≪1Kp\ll 1:

P⁡(Ny≥1)≈K​πt​(y|x)P(N_{y}\geq 1)\approx K\pi_{t}(y|x)

When πt​(y|x)≪1/K\pi_{t}(y|x)\ll 1/K, we have P⁡(Ny≥1)≪1P(N_{y}\geq 1)\ll 1, meaning yy is almost never sampled.

Without samples, the gradient contribution from yy is zero, and πt​(y|x)\pi_{t}(y|x) can only decrease (due to the softmax normalization as other solutions increase). The expected waiting time for at least one sample is 1/ℙ⁡(Ny≥1)=Ω⁡(1/(K​p))1/\mathbb{P}(N_{y}\geq 1)=\Omega(1/(Kp)). This makes the collapse irreversible. ∎

A.3 Proofs for uniform-correct optimality

Theorem A.3 (Robustness under distribution shift).

Suppose a distribution shift disables a subset S⊂𝒴+S\subset\mathcal{Y}^{+} of correct outputs, where |S|≤s|S|\leq s. Consider the robust objective:

maxπminS:|S|≤s∑y∈𝒴+∖Sπ(y|x).\max_{\pi}\min_{S:|S|\leq s}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}\setminus S}\pi(y|x). (26)

Then the uniform distribution over 𝒴+\mathcal{Y}^{+} uniquely maximizes the worst-case retained probability mass.

Proof.

Let π\pi be any distribution over 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x) with ∑y∈𝒴+​(x)π⁡(y|x)=1\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi(y|x)=1. The adversary choosing SS will select the ss outputs with highest probability mass.

For the uniform distribution π∗​(y|x)=1/|𝒴+|\pi^{*}(y|x)=1/|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|, the worst-case retained mass is:

1−s|𝒴+​(x)|.1-\frac{s}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|}. (27)

For any non-uniform distribution, let

πmax=maxy∈𝒴+⁡π⁡(y|x)>1|𝒴+​(x)|.\pi_{\max}=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi(y|x)>\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|}.

The adversary can achieve retained mass strictly less than 1−s/|𝒴+​(x)|1-s/|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)| by targeting high-probability outputs.

Sorting probabilities in decreasing order:

π⁡(y(1)|x)≥π⁡(y(2)|x)≥…\pi(y_{(1)}|x)\geq\pi(y_{(2)}|x)\geq\ldots

the adversary removes {y(1),…,y(s)}\{y_{(1)},\ldots,y_{(s)}\}, achieving retained mass:

∑j>sπ⁡(y(j)|x)=1−∑j=1sπ⁡(y(j)|x)≤1−s|𝒴+​(x)|,\sum_{j>s}\pi(y_{(j)}|x)=1-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\pi(y_{(j)}|x)\leq 1-\frac{s}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|}, (28)

with equality if and only if π\pi is uniform. Thus, the uniform distribution over 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x) uniquely maximizes the worst-case retained probability mass. ∎

Theorem A.4.

Consider the entropy-regularized objective

maxπ(⋅∣x)𝔼y∼π[R(x,y)]+τH(π(⋅∣x)).\max_{\pi(\cdot\mid x)}\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[R(x,y)]+\tau\,\mathrm{H}(\pi(\cdot\mid x)). (29)

There exists a threshold τ0>0\tau_{0}>0 such that for all 0<τ<τ00<\tau<\tau_{0}, any optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} places zero mass on incorrect outputs and is uniform over 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x).

Proof.

Let R⁡(x,y)∈{0,1}R(x,y)\in\{0,1\} and 𝒴+​(x)={y:R⁡(x,y)=1}\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)=\{y:R(x,y)=1\} is non-empty and not equal to the full output space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Let 𝒴−=𝒴∖𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{-}=\mathcal{Y}\setminus\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x) denote incorrect outputs. Taking the objective as

J⁡(π)=Z⁡(x)+τ​H​(π),Z⁡(x)=∑y∈𝒴+π⁡(y∣x).J(\pi)=Z(x)+\tau H(\pi),\qquad Z(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi(y\mid x).
Step 1: Support concentrates on correct outputs for small τ\tau.

Suppose π\pi assigns mass ϵ>0\epsilon>0 to 𝒴−\mathcal{Y}^{-}. Construct a new policy π~\tilde{\pi} by moving this mass to any correct output y+∈𝒴+y^{+}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}.

The reward change is

Δ​Z=Z⁡(π~)−Z⁡(π)=ϵ.\Delta Z=Z(\tilde{\pi})-Z(\pi)=\epsilon.

Moving probability mass between two outcomes changes entropy by at most O⁡(ϵ​log⁡|𝒴|)O(\epsilon\log|\mathcal{Y}|), so

J⁡(π~)−J⁡(π)≥ϵ−τ​C​ϵJ(\tilde{\pi})-J(\pi)\geq\epsilon-\tau C\epsilon

for some constant C≤log⁡|𝒴|C\leq\log|\mathcal{Y}|. If τ<1/C\tau<1/C, transferring mass from incorrect to correct strictly improves the objective. Therefore any maximizer must satisfy Z⁡(x)=1Z(x)=1, i.e., π⁡(y∣x)=0\pi(y\mid x)=0 for all y∈𝒴−y\in\mathcal{Y}^{-}.

Step 2: Uniformity within the correct set.

Given Z⁡(x)=1Z(x)=1, the objective reduces to

J⁡(π)=1+τ​H​(π),J(\pi)=1+\tau H(\pi),

with π\pi supported on 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x). Let q⁡(y∣x)=π⁡(y∣x)q(y\mid x)=\pi(y\mid x) for y∈𝒴+​(x)y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x). Then

maxq⁡H⁡(q)s.t.∑y∈𝒴+​(x)q⁡(y∣x)=1.\max_{q}H(q)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}q(y\mid x)=1.

Entropy is strictly concave, so the unique maximizer is the uniform distribution:

q∗​(y∣x)=1|𝒴+​(x)|.q^{*}(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|}.

Thus, for sufficiently small τ\tau, the optimal entropy-regularized policy is uniform over correct outputs. ∎

A.4 Proof of Gradient Decomposition Proposition  6.1

Proposition A.2 (Gradient Decomposition, restated).

Let xx be a prompt with 𝒴+​(x)≠∅\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)\neq\emptyset. Define the correctness mass Zθ​(x)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)πθ​(y∣x)Z_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x), the conditional distribution qθ​(y∣x)=πθ​(y∣x)/Zθ​(x)q_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)/Z_{\theta}(x), and the uniform distribution u⁡(y∣x)=1/|𝒴+​(x)|u(y\mid x)=1/|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|. Then the gradient of the UCPO objective (excluding the reference KL term) is:

∇θLUCPO​(x)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)[(1−τ)​qθ​(y∣x)+τ​u​(y∣x)]​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y∣x).\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\Big[(1-\tau)\,q_{\theta}(y\mid x)+\tau\,u(y\mid x)\Big]\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x).
Proof.

We compute the gradients of each term in LUCPO(x)=logZθ(x)−τKL(u∥qθ)L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x)=\log Z_{\theta}(x)-\tau\,\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}) separately.

Step 1: Gradient of log⁡Zθ​(x)\log Z_{\theta}(x).

By the chain rule,

∇θ​log​Zθ​(x)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x) =1Zθ​(x)​∇θZθ​(x)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{\theta}(x)}\nabla_{\theta}Z_{\theta}(x) (30)
=1Zθ​(x)​∑y∈𝒴+​(x)∇θπθ​(y∣x)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{\theta}(x)}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x) (31)
=1Zθ​(x)​∑y∈𝒴+​(x)πθ​(y∣x)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y∣x)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{\theta}(x)}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x) (32)
=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)qθ​(y∣x)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y∣x).\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}q_{\theta}(y\mid x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x). (33)
Step 2: Gradient of KL(u∥qθ)\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}).

Expanding the KL divergence,

KL(u∥qθ)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}) =∑y∈𝒴+​(x)u⁡(y∣x)​log⁡u⁡(y∣x)qθ​(y∣x)\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}u(y\mid x)\log\frac{u(y\mid x)}{q_{\theta}(y\mid x)} (34)
=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)u⁡(y∣x)​log⁡u⁡(y∣x)−∑y∈𝒴+​(x)u⁡(y∣x)​log​qθ​(y∣x).\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}u(y\mid x)\log u(y\mid x)-\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}u(y\mid x)\log q_{\theta}(y\mid x). (35)

The first sum is a constant (entropy of uu), so

∇θKL(u∥qθ)=−∑y∈𝒴+​(x)u(y∣x)∇θlogqθ(y∣x).\nabla_{\theta}\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta})=-\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}u(y\mid x)\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y\mid x).
Step 3: Gradient of log⁡qθ​(y∣x)\log q_{\theta}(y\mid x).

Since qθ​(y∣x)=πθ​(y∣x)/Zθ​(x)q_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)/Z_{\theta}(x),

∇θ​log​qθ​(y∣x)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y\mid x) =∇θ​log​πθ​(y∣x)−∇θ​log​Zθ​(x).\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)-\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x). (36)
Step 4: Combining.

Substituting Step 3 into Step 2:

∇θKL(u∥qθ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}) =−∑yu(y)[∇θlogπθ(y)−∇θlogZθ(x)]\displaystyle=-\sum_{y}u(y)\Big[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)-\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x)\Big] (37)
=−∑yu(y)∇θlogπθ(y)+∇θlogZθ(x),\displaystyle=-\sum_{y}u(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)+\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x), (38)

where we used ∑yu⁡(y)=1\sum_{y}u(y)=1.

Therefore,

∇θ[−τKL(u∥qθ)]\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\big[-\tau\,\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta})\big] =τ​∑yu⁡(y)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y)−τ​∇θ​log⁡Zθ​(x).\displaystyle=\tau\sum_{y}u(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)-\tau\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x). (39)
Step 5: Full gradient.

Adding the gradients from Steps 1 and 4:

∇θLUCPO​(x)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x) =∇θ​log​Zθ​(x)+τ​∑yu⁡(y)​∇θ​log​πθ​(y)−τ​∇θ​log​Zθ​(x)\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x)+\tau\sum_{y}u(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)-\tau\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x) (40)
=(1−τ)​∇θ​log⁡Zθ​(x)+τ​∑yu⁡(y)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y)\displaystyle=(1-\tau)\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x)+\tau\sum_{y}u(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y) (41)
=(1−τ)​∑yqθ​(y)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y)+τ​∑yu⁡(y)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y)\displaystyle=(1-\tau)\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)+\tau\sum_{y}u(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y) (42)
=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)[(1−τ)​qθ​(y)+τ​u​(y)]​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y).∎\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\Big[(1-\tau)q_{\theta}(y)+\tau u(y)\Big]\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y).\qed (43)

A.5 Derivation of the Inverse-q Importance Weights

We know the gradient weights each correct response by a convex combination of its current conditional probability qθ​(y)q_{\theta}(y) and the uniform weight u⁡(y)u(y). Rewriting as expectations:

∇θLUCPO=(1−τ)​𝔼y∼qθ​[∇θ​log​πθ​(y∣x)]+τ​𝔼y∼u​[∇θ​log​πθ​(y∣x)].\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}=(1-\tau)\,\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)]+\tau\,\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)]. (44)

We estimate the terms from the nn correct rollouts {yi}i=1n∼qθ(⋅∣x)\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) out of the sampled N rollouts from πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) . The first term is an expectation under qθq_{\theta}, estimated directly as a sample mean:

𝔼y∼qθ​[∇θ​log​πθ​(y)]≈1n​∑i=1n∇θ​log​πθ​(yi∣x).\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)]\approx\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x). (45)

The second term is an expectation under the uniform distribution uu, but we only have samples from qθq_{\theta}. So, we derive the importance sampling estimator for 𝔼y∼u​[f​(y)]\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}[f(y)] using samples from qθq_{\theta}.

Importance sampling identity.

For any function ff,

𝔼y∼u​[f⁡(y)]=𝔼y∼qθ​[u⁡(y)qθ​(y)​f​(y)].\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}[f(y)]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q_{\theta}}\left[\frac{u(y)}{q_{\theta}(y)}f(y)\right]. (46)
Simplifying the importance ratio.

Since u⁡(y)=1/|𝒴+​(x)|u(y)=1/|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)| is constant over the correct set,

u⁡(y)qθ​(y)=1|𝒴+​(x)|⋅1qθ​(y).\frac{u(y)}{q_{\theta}(y)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|}\cdot\frac{1}{q_{\theta}(y)}. (47)

The factor 1/|𝒴+​(x)|1/|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)| is independent of yy and cancels under normalization. Thus, the importance weight is proportional to 1/qθ​(y)1/q_{\theta}(y). Given samples {yi}i=1n∼qθ\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim q_{\theta}, the unnormalized importance sampling estimator is

𝔼y∼u​[f⁡(y)]≈1n⋅|𝒴+​(x)|​∑i=1n1qθ​(yi)​f​(yi).\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}[f(y)]\approx\frac{1}{n\cdot|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{q_{\theta}(y_{i})}f(y_{i}).

However, we do not know |𝒴+​(x)||\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)| or qθ​(yi)q_{\theta}(y_{i}) exactly.

Self-normalized estimator.

Given samples {yi}i=1n∼qθ\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim q_{\theta}, we estimate qθ​(yi)q_{\theta}(y_{i}) empirically:

q^i=πθ​(yi∣x)∑j=1nπθ​(yj∣x).\hat{q}_{i}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\pi_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid x)}. (48)

Define unnormalized weights vi=1/q^iv_{i}=1/\hat{q}_{i}. The self-normalized importance sampling estimator is:

𝔼y∼u​[f⁡(y)]≈∑i=1nvi∑j=1nvj​f​(yi).\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}[f(y)]\approx\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{v_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}}f(y_{i}). (49)
𝔼y∼u​[∇θ​log​πθ​(y)]≈∑i=1nvi∑j=1nvj​∇θ​log​πθ​(yi∣x).\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)]\approx\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{v_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x). (50)

Self-normalization avoids needing to know |𝒴+​(x)||\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)| and ensures bounded weights. It introduces O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) bias but significantly reduces variance compared to unnormalized importance sampling, which is critical when q^i\hat{q}_{i} may be small for rare correct responses.

Combining both terms yields the UCPO gradient estimator:

∇θLUCPO≈∑i=1nwi​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣x),\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}\approx\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x), (51)

where

wi=1−τn+τ⋅vi∑j=1nvj.w_{i}=\frac{1-\tau}{n}+\tau\cdot\frac{v_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}}. (52)

Responses with high qθ​(yi)q_{\theta}(y_{i}) (already favored by the policy) receive low weight viv_{i}. Responses with low qθ​(yi)q_{\theta}(y_{i}) (rare under current policy) receive high weight. This reweighting transforms samples from qθq_{\theta} into an approximation of uniform samples over the correct set.

A.6 Proofs for Proposition  6.2 and Theorem  6.1

Proposition A.3 (Mass Preservation, restated).

Let AbaseA_{\mathrm{base}} be the GRPO advantage for correct responses, and let nn be the number of correct rollouts. Define UCPO advantages as AiUCPO=Abase⋅n⋅wiblendA_{i}^{\mathrm{UCPO}}=A_{\mathrm{base}}\cdot n\cdot w_{i}^{\mathrm{blend}} where

wiblend=1−τn+τ⋅vi∑j=1nvj.w_{i}^{\mathrm{blend}}=\frac{1-\tau}{n}+\tau\cdot\frac{v_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}}.

Then:

∑i=1nAiUCPO=∑i=1nAiGRPO=n⋅Abase.\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{\mathrm{UCPO}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=n\cdot A_{\mathrm{base}}.
Proof.

We verify that the blended weights sum to one:

∑i=1nwiblend\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}^{\mathrm{blend}} =∑i=1n(1−τn+τ⋅vi∑j=1nvj)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1-\tau}{n}+\tau\cdot\frac{v_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}}\right) (53)
=(1−τ)⋅nn+τ⋅∑i=1nvi∑j=1nvj\displaystyle=(1-\tau)\cdot\frac{n}{n}+\tau\cdot\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}} (54)
=(1−τ)+τ\displaystyle=(1-\tau)+\tau (55)
=1.\displaystyle=1. (56)

Therefore,

∑i=1nAiUCPO=Abase⋅n⋅∑i=1nwiblend=Abase⋅n⋅1=n⋅Abase.\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{\mathrm{UCPO}}=A_{\mathrm{base}}\cdot n\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}^{\mathrm{blend}}=A_{\mathrm{base}}\cdot n\cdot 1=n\cdot A_{\mathrm{base}}.

Standard GRPO assigns AbaseA_{\mathrm{base}} to each of the nn correct responses, so ∑iAiGRPO=n⋅Abase\sum_{i}A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=n\cdot A_{\mathrm{base}}. ∎

Theorem A.5 (Uniform-correct policy uniquely maximizes the UCPO objective).

For a fixed prompt xx, consider the UCPO objective without the reference KL term:

LUCPO(x)=logZθ(x)−τKL(u(⋅∣x)∥qθ(⋅∣x)),L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x)=\log Z_{\theta}(x)-\tau\,\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(u(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr),

where

Zθ​(x)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)πθ​(y∣x),qθ​(y∣x)=πθ​(y∣x)Zθ​(x)for ​y∈𝒴+​(x),Z_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x),\qquad q_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{Z_{\theta}(x)}\quad\text{for }y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x),

and

u⁡(y∣x)=1|𝒴+​(x)|for ​y∈𝒴+​(x).u(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|}\quad\text{for }y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x).

For any τ>0\tau>0, the unique maximizer of LUCPO​(x)L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x) over policies πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) is the uniform-correct policy

π∗​(y∣x)={1|𝒴+​(x)|,y∈𝒴+​(x),0,y∉𝒴+​(x).\pi^{*}(y\mid x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|},&y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x),\\[4.0pt] 0,&y\notin\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x).\end{cases}
Proof.

For any policy πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), since πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) is a probability distribution over the full output space,

Zθ​(x)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)πθ​(y∣x)≤1.Z_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\leq 1.

Therefore,

log⁡Zθ​(x)≤0,\log Z_{\theta}(x)\leq 0,

with equality if and only if Zθ​(x)=1Z_{\theta}(x)=1, i.e., if and only if

πθ​(y∣x)=0for all ​y∉𝒴+​(x).\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=0\qquad\text{for all }y\notin\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x).

Next, by non-negativity of KL divergence,

KL(u(⋅∣x)∥qθ(⋅∣x))≥0,\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(u(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)\geq 0,

so

−τKL(u(⋅∣x)∥qθ(⋅∣x))≤0,-\tau\,\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(u(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)\leq 0,

with equality if and only if

qθ(⋅∣x)=u(⋅∣x).q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)=u(\cdot\mid x).

Combining the two inequalities,

LUCPO(x)=logZθ(x)−τKL(u(⋅∣x)∥qθ(⋅∣x))≤0.L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x)=\log Z_{\theta}(x)-\tau\,\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(u(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)\leq 0.

Equality holds if and only if both conditions are satisfied:

  1. 1.

    Zθ​(x)=1Z_{\theta}(x)=1, so all probability mass lies on 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x); and

  2. 2.

    qθ(⋅∣x)=u(⋅∣x)q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)=u(\cdot\mid x), so the conditional distribution over correct responses is uniform.

These two conditions uniquely determine

πθ​(y∣x)={1|𝒴+​(x)|,y∈𝒴+​(x),0,y∉𝒴+​(x),\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|},&y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x),\\[4.0pt] 0,&y\notin\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x),\end{cases}

which is exactly the uniform-correct policy π∗\pi^{*}. Hence π∗\pi^{*} is the unique maximizer of LUCPO​(x)L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}(x). ∎

A.7 Choice of Divergence

The UCPO objective penalizes deviation from the uniform target using KL(u∥qθ)\mathrm{KL}(u\,\|\,q_{\theta}) rather than KL(qθ∥u)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\theta}\,\|\,u). While both divergences are minimized when qθ=uq_{\theta}=u, their gradients differ in a way that is critical for escaping mode collapse. We derive the gradient of each and explain why KL(u∥qθ)\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}) is the appropriate choice.

A.7.1 Entropy Maximization: KL(qθ∥u)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\theta}\,\|\,u)

When uu is uniform over 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x), we have log⁡u⁡(y)=−log⁡|𝒴+​(x)|\log u(y)=-\log|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)| for all y∈𝒴+​(x)y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x). Expanding the KL divergence:

KL(qθ∥u)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(q_{\theta}\|u) =∑y∈𝒴+​(x)qθ​(y)​log⁡qθ​(y)u⁡(y)\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}q_{\theta}(y)\log\frac{q_{\theta}(y)}{u(y)} (57)
=∑yqθ​(y)​log⁡qθ​(y)−∑yqθ​(y)​log⁡u⁡(y)\displaystyle=\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)\log q_{\theta}(y)-\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)\log u(y) (58)
=−H⁡(qθ)+log⁡|𝒴+​(x)|.\displaystyle=-H(q_{\theta})+\log|\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)|. (59)

Thus, minimizing KL(qθ∥u)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\theta}\|u) is equivalent to maximizing the entropy H⁡(qθ)H(q_{\theta}).

The entropy of qθq_{\theta} is:

H(qθ)=−∑y∈𝒴+​(x)qθ(y)logqθ(y).H(q_{\theta})=-\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}q_{\theta}(y)\log q_{\theta}(y).

Taking the gradient with respect to θ\theta:

∇θH​(qθ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}H(q_{\theta}) =−∑y∇θ[qθ(y)logqθ(y)]\displaystyle=-\sum_{y}\nabla_{\theta}\big[q_{\theta}(y)\log q_{\theta}(y)\big] (60)
=−∑y[∇θqθ(y)⋅logqθ(y)+qθ(y)⋅∇θlogqθ(y)]\displaystyle=-\sum_{y}\big[\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}(y)\cdot\log q_{\theta}(y)+q_{\theta}(y)\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y)\big] (61)
=−∑y∇θqθ(y)⋅logqθ(y)−∑yqθ(y)∇θlogqθ(y).\displaystyle=-\sum_{y}\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}(y)\cdot\log q_{\theta}(y)-\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y). (62)

Since ∑yqθ​(y)=1\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)=1, we have ∑y∇θqθ​(y)=0\sum_{y}\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}(y)=0. Using ∇θqθ​(y)=qθ​(y)​∇θ​log⁡qθ​(y)\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}(y)=q_{\theta}(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y):

∇θH​(qθ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}H(q_{\theta}) =−∑yqθ(y)∇θlogqθ(y)⋅logqθ(y)−∑yqθ(y)∇θlogqθ(y)\displaystyle=-\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y)\cdot\log q_{\theta}(y)-\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y) (63)
=−∑yqθ(y)[1+logqθ(y)]∇θlogqθ(y)\displaystyle=-\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)\big[1+\log q_{\theta}(y)\big]\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y) (64)
=−𝔼y∼qθ​[(1+log⁡qθ​(y))​∇θ​log⁡qθ​(y)].\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q_{\theta}}\big[(1+\log q_{\theta}(y))\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}(y)\big]. (65)

The gradient is weighted by the current distribution qθq_{\theta}. High-probability responses dominate the gradient; low-probability responses contribute negligibly. This preserves the feedback loop identified in Section 4.2: frequently sampled solutions receive larger updates, reinforcing their dominance.

A.7.2 Uniform-Weighted Divergence: KL(u∥qθ)\mathrm{KL}(u\,\|\,q_{\theta})

Expanding the KL divergence:

KL(u∥qθ)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}) =∑y∈𝒴+​(x)u⁡(y)​log⁡u⁡(y)qθ​(y)\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}u(y)\log\frac{u(y)}{q_{\theta}(y)} (66)
=∑yu⁡(y)​log⁡u⁡(y)−∑yu⁡(y)​log​qθ​(y)\displaystyle=\sum_{y}u(y)\log u(y)-\sum_{y}u(y)\log q_{\theta}(y) (67)
=−H⁡(u)−∑yu⁡(y)​log⁡qθ​(y).\displaystyle=-H(u)-\sum_{y}u(y)\log q_{\theta}(y). (68)

Since H⁡(u)H(u) is constant with respect to θ\theta:

−KL(u∥qθ)=∑yu(y)logqθ(y)+const.-\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta})=\sum_{y}u(y)\log q_{\theta}(y)+\mathrm{const}.

Substituting qθ​(y)=πθ​(y)/Zθ​(x)q_{\theta}(y)=\pi_{\theta}(y)/Z_{\theta}(x) where Zθ​(x)=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)πθ​(y)Z_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\pi_{\theta}(y):

−KL(u∥qθ)\displaystyle-\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}) =∑yu⁡(y)​[log⁡πθ​(y)−log⁡Zθ​(x)]+const\displaystyle=\sum_{y}u(y)\big[\log\pi_{\theta}(y)-\log Z_{\theta}(x)\big]+\mathrm{const} (69)
=∑yu⁡(y)​log⁡πθ​(y)−log⁡Zθ​(x)+const.\displaystyle=\sum_{y}u(y)\log\pi_{\theta}(y)-\log Z_{\theta}(x)+\mathrm{const}. (70)

Taking the gradient:

∇θ[−KL(u∥qθ)]\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\big[-\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta})\big] =∑yu⁡(y)​∇θ​log​πθ​(y)−∇θ​log​Zθ​(x).\displaystyle=\sum_{y}u(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)-\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x). (71)

For the second term, we use:

∇θ​log​Zθ​(x)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\log Z_{\theta}(x) =1Zθ​(x)​∑y∈𝒴+​(x)∇θπθ​(y)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{\theta}(x)}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y) (72)
=∑yπθ​(y)Zθ​(x)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y)\displaystyle=\sum_{y}\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y)}{Z_{\theta}(x)}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y) (73)
=∑yqθ​(y)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y).\displaystyle=\sum_{y}q_{\theta}(y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y). (74)

Substituting:

∇θ[−KL(u∥qθ)]=𝔼y∼u[∇θlogπθ(y)]−𝔼y∼qθ[∇θlogπθ(y)].\nabla_{\theta}\big[-\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta})\big]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}\big[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)\big]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q_{\theta}}\big[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)\big]. (75)

The gradient consists of two terms:

  • •

    𝔼y∼u​[∇θ​log​πθ​(y)]\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)]: Increases probability of all correct responses equally, regardless of their current probability.

  • •

    −𝔼y∼qθ​[∇θ​log​πθ​(y)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y)]: Decreases probability of responses in proportion to their current dominance.

Together, these terms redistribute gradient signal from overrepresented to underrepresented responses, breaking the self-reinforcing feedback loop.

A.7.3 Connection to UCPO

Combining KL(u∥qθ)\mathrm{KL}(u\|q_{\theta}) with the correctness objective log⁡Zθ​(x)\log Z_{\theta}(x) yields the UCPO gradient (Proposition 6.1):

∇θLUCPO=∑y∈𝒴+​(x)[(1−τ)​qθ​(y)+τ​u​(y)]​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y∣x).\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{UCPO}}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x)}\big[(1-\tau)\,q_{\theta}(y)+\tau\,u(y)\big]\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x).

At τ=0\tau=0, updates are fully qθq_{\theta}-weighted (GRPO). As τ\tau increases, updates shift toward uniform weighting, directly counteracting the sampling bias that drives collapse.

Appendix B Controlled Empirical Validation of Collapse Dynamics

Section  4.2 establishes that diversity collapse under RLVR arises from the interaction between objective indifference and optimization dynamics, which together induce a self-reinforcing concentration of probability mass on a subset of correct solutions. While this mechanism is derived analytically, its empirical manifestation in large-scale language models is difficult to observe directly due to partial observability and sequence-level complexity.

To isolate and validate the proposed mechanism, we construct a controlled RLVR environment in which the policy is fully observable and all quantities can be computed exactly. The goal of this experiment is to causally verify each component of the collapse mechanism under minimal assumptions.

Setup.

We define a discrete output space of 20 tokens, among which a subset of 3 tokens are designated as correct:

𝒴+={y1,y2,y3},𝒴−=𝒴∖𝒴+.\mathcal{Y}^{+}=\{y_{1},y_{2},y_{3}\},\qquad\mathcal{Y}^{-}=\mathcal{Y}\setminus\mathcal{Y}^{+}.

The policy πθ​(y)\pi_{\theta}(y) is parameterized as a softmax over logits zyz_{y}:

πθ​(y)=exp⁡(zy)∑y′exp⁡(zy′).\pi_{\theta}(y)=\frac{\exp(z_{y})}{\sum_{y^{\prime}}\exp(z_{y^{\prime}})}.

To reflect realistic pretrained biases, the initial policy assigns non-uniform probability mass within the correct set, while distributing the remaining mass across incorrect outputs. This ensures that symmetry is broken at initialization, allowing us to study how small imbalances evolve under training.

Training Dynamics.

At each iteration:

  • •

    We sample KK outputs from πθ\pi_{\theta} (on-policy sampling).

  • •

    Rewards are assigned deterministically:

    R(y)=𝟏[y∈𝒴+].R(y)=\mathbf{1}[y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}].
  • •

    The policy is updated using either GRPO, UCPO, and Global entropy regularization.

Tracked Metrics.

Since the full distribution is explicitly available, we analyze training dynamics through the following quantities:

(i) Sampling statistics. The number of times each output is sampled: NyN_{y}.

(ii) Conditional distribution over correct solutions. We define the normalized distribution restricted to correct outputs:

qθ​(y∣𝒴+)=πθ​(y)∑y′∈𝒴+πθ​(y′),y∈𝒴+.q_{\theta}(y\mid\mathcal{Y}^{+})=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y)}{\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime})},\quad y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}.

(iii) Entropy of correct solutions. To measure diversity within the correct set:

H(qθ)=−∑y∈𝒴+qθ(y∣𝒴+)logqθ(y∣𝒴+).H(q_{\theta})=-\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}q_{\theta}(y\mid\mathcal{Y}^{+})\log q_{\theta}(y\mid\mathcal{Y}^{+}).

(iv) Total correctness mass. The probability assigned to correct outputs:

Zθ=∑y∈𝒴+πθ​(y).Z_{\theta}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi_{\theta}(y).

(v) Relative dominance. We monitor pairwise probability ratios between correct solutions to capture mode concentration:

πθ​(yi)πθ​(yj),yi,yj∈𝒴+.\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{j})},\quad y_{i},y_{j}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}.

B.1 GRPO Induces Self-Reinforcing Collapse

We validate each step of the collapse mechanism (Section 5), with the corresponding evidence shown in Figure  1.

  1. 1.

    Sampling bias: Figure  1(a) shows that higher-probability solutions are sampled more frequently, with empirical counts closely matching theoretical expectation:

    𝔼⁡[Ny]=K⋅πθ​(y).\mathbb{E}[N_{y}]=K\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y).

    Even under near-uniform initialization (Appendix  B.2), stochastic sampling produces unequal counts, confirming the inherent bias of on-policy estimation.

  2. 2.

    Gradient amplification: Figure  1(b) plots f⁡(p)=p⁡(1−p)f(p)=p(1-p), the function proportional to the expected gradient magnitude for a softmax policy. The green dots mark the initial probabilities of the three correct tokens. The key observation is that tokens already at higher probability receive a larger expected gradient update. Under GRPO, all correct samples receive the same normalized advantage A+A^{+}, so the total expected update to log⁡π⁡(y)\log\pi(y) scales as:

    Δ​log⁡πθ​(y)∝η⋅A+⋅K⋅πθ​(y).\Delta\log\pi_{\theta}(y)\propto\eta\cdot A^{+}\cdot K\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y).

    This confirms that GRPO amplifies sampling asymmetries rather than correcting them.

  3. 3.

    Probability ratios diverge monotonically. Figure  1(c) tracks the evolution of probability ratios between correct solutions. The log-ratio between dominant and minority solutions increases steadily over training:

    log⁡πθ​(y1)πθ​(y2)↑.\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{1})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{2})}\uparrow.

    This demonstrates the positive feedback loop predicted in Theorem  4.3, that the expected change in log-ratio is proportional to the difference in probabilities, which is always positive when y0≥y1y_{0}\geq y_{1}.

  4. 4.

    Collapse is irreversible once below the sampling threshold. Figure  1(d) shows the conditional distribution

    qθ​(y∣correct)=πθ​(y)Zθq_{\theta}(y\mid\text{correct})=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y)}{Z_{\theta}}

    at five snapshots during training (steps 0,50,100,200,2990,50,100,200,299). The blue dashed line marks the uniform target 1/31/3. By step 299299, virtually all mass has migrated to y0y_{0}. The solutions y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} fall so far below the sampling threshold (𝔼⁡[Ny]≪1\mathbb{E}[N_{y}]\ll 1) that they receive negligible gradient signal and can no longer recover. This confirms the irreversibility predicted in Corollary  4.1.

B.2 Collapse Is Not Limited to Skewed Initializations

In Figure 1, we use a skewed initialization of 4:2:14:2:1 over correct tokens to make the collapse dynamics visually clear. However, even under near-uniform initialization, stochastic sampling produces unequal counts, confirming the inherent bias of on-policy estimation, consistent with Proposition 4.1. To verify this we evaluate three initialization profiles spanning the range from maximally symmetric to strongly biased. The reference policy assigns background mass 0.010.01 to each incorrect token (before normalization) across all profiles:

  • •

    Uniform (1:1:1): qθ​(y0)=qθ​(y1)=qθ​(y2)=0.333q_{\theta}(y_{0})=q_{\theta}(y_{1})=q_{\theta}(y_{2})=0.333. Tests the null hypothesis that collapse requires an initial imbalance.

  • •

    Mild skew (1.5:1.2:1): qθ​(y0)=0.41,qθ​(y1)=0.32,qθ​(y2)=0.27q_{\theta}(y_{0})=0.41,\;q_{\theta}(y_{1})=0.32,\;q_{\theta}(y_{2})=0.27. Reflects the small asymmetry.

  • •

    Skewed (4:2:1): qθ​(y0)=0.57,qθ​(y1)=0.29,qθ​(y2)=0.14q_{\theta}(y_{0})=0.57,\;q_{\theta}(y_{1})=0.29,\;q_{\theta}(y_{2})=0.14.

We run 5 independent seeds per profile and track the conditional entropy H⁡(qθ)H(q_{\theta}) and correctness mass ZθZ_{\theta} throughout training. Results are shown in Figure 2. Under skewed and mild-skew initialization, the dominant token y0y_{0} wins deterministically across all 5 seeds: GRPO always amplifies the initially more-probable correct token, confirming the collapse mechanism. Final conditional entropy is H⁡(qθ)/Hmax≈16%H(q_{\theta})/H_{\mathrm{max}}\approx 16\% (skewed) and 32%32\% (mild skew), both far below the uniform target.

Under uniform initialization, collapse still occurs in every seed, but the winner is arbitrary: across 5 seeds, y0y_{0} collapses to the dominant mode in 3 runs, y1y_{1} in 1 run, and y2y_{2} in 1 run. This is a direct consequence of Proposition A.1 (stochastic symmetry breaking): even when π0​(y∣x)=1/|Y+|\pi_{0}(y\mid x)=1/|Y^{+}|, finite-batch sampling produces unequal counts {Ny}\{N_{y}\} with probability 1, seeding the positive feedback loop. GRPO then amplifies whichever token happened to be over-represented in the first batch.

These results establish that mode collapse is not an artifact of a skewed initialization, it is an intrinsic consequence of the interaction between on-policy sampling variance and GRPO’s indifference to within-correct diversity. The skewed profile collapses faster and more predictably; the uniform profile collapses more slowly and to an arbitrary mode.

GRPO Induces Concentration within the Correct Set

We further analyze the training dynamics of GRPO, UCPO, and global entropy regularization in depth (Figure 3). As shown in Figure 3(a), GRPO drives the conditional distribution qθ​(y∣𝒴+)q_{\theta}(y\mid\mathcal{Y}^{+}) toward a single dominant solution. Correspondingly, Figure 3(d) shows rapid decay in conditional entropy H⁡(qθ)H(q_{\theta}), while Figure 3(e) shows that total correctness mass ZZ remains high.

This indicates that GRPO improves correctness by concentrating probability mass rather than maintaining coverage over multiple valid solutions while UCPO and Global entropy regularization maintain a balance distribution. As a result, diversity within the correct set collapses despite high sampling efficiency.

B.3 UCPO Preserves Diversity via Gradient Redistribution

UCPO modifies training dynamics by redistributing gradient signal within the correct set according to the reweighting mechanism derived in Section  6.

As shown in Figure 3(a), UCPO maintains a balanced conditional distribution: qθ​(y∣𝒴+)≈uniform.q_{\theta}(y\mid\mathcal{Y}^{+})\approx\text{uniform}. Figure 3(d) shows that conditional entropy remains high throughout training, while Figure 3(e) shows that correctness mass ZZ is preserved.

To isolate the mechanism of UCPO, we further analyze gradient contributions per solution. Figure 4(b) shows that UCPO equalizes gradient contributions across correct solutions and removes the implicit bias toward dominant modes while preserving total gradient mass. In contrast to GRPO where contributions scale with sample count (Figure 4(a)), leads to dominance of frequently sampled solutions.

These results demonstrate that UCPO counteracts the sampling-induced imbalance by redistributing updates within the correct set, preventing concentration while maintaining correctness.

B.4 Global Entropy Regularization Increases Entropy on the Wrong Support

We analyze global entropy regularization in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

Figure 3(d) shows that entropy regularization increases overall entropy, but Figure 3(f) reveals that this increase is partly driven by probability mass assigned to incorrect outputs.

Figure 5(b) further shows that as τent\tau_{\text{ent}} increases, the equilibrium mass on incorrect tokens grows monotonically. Since the entropy bonus is applied uniformly across all outputs, it provides equal incentive to increase the probability on incorrect and underrepresented correct solutions.

As a result, Figure 5(c) shows that improvements in entropy H⁡(qθ)H(q_{\theta}) come at the cost of reduced correctness mass ZθZ_{\theta}. This confirms that global entropy regularization increases entropy on the wrong support and cannot preserve diversity within the correct set.

B.5 UCPO Maintains Correctness–Diversity Trade-off

Figure 6 shows that increasing τ\tau improves diversity while preserving correctness. Unlike entropy regularization, the mass on incorrect outputs remains negligible across all τ\tau, and ZθZ_{\theta} remains close to 1.0.

This demonstrates that UCPO can increase diversity without incurring the correctness trade-off observed in global entropy methods.

Appendix C Why Global entropy regularization fails

A direct way to operationalize the entropy-regularized criterion from Section 5 is to add a global entropy bonus to the RLVR objective:

Jent(π)=𝔼y∼π[R(x,y)]+τent⋅H(π(⋅∣x)).J_{\mathrm{ent}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}\!\left[R(x,y)\right]+\tau_{\text{ent}}\cdot H\!\left(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\right). (76)

Although this objective can recover the Uniform-Correct Policy for a suitable choice of τ\tau (Theorem 5.2), it does not reliably recover UCP in practice. The coefficient τ\tau is difficult to tune (Table  3), and for suboptimal values the optimal policy need not remain uniform-correct. Further, the induced optimization dynamics do not directly target balanced allocation within the correct set.

First, the entropy term is computed over the full output space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, including incorrect solutions, rather than within the correct set 𝒴+​(x)\mathcal{Y}^{+}(x). The reward term pushes mass toward correct outputs, while the entropy term pushes mass toward all outputs indiscriminately. This creates a structural trade-off: diversity is encouraged on the wrong support. Empirically, global entropy regularization increases overall entropy but does not improve diversity within the correct set (Section 7.3), with much of the entropy increase arising from mass allocated to incorrect outputs (Appendix B.4).

Second, under GRPO with binary rewards, when all rollouts for a prompt are correct (or all incorrect), the group-normalized advantages are Ai=0A_{i}=0 for every rollout. In this case, the reward term contributes no gradient, and the update is driven entirely by the entropy bonus. The policy is then pushed to spread mass across all outputs, including incorrect ones, rather than preserving diversity within the correct set. This failure mode is particularly common for easier prompts, where the model achieves high accuracy early in training. Thus, global entropy regularization fails to approximate the optimum of Eq. (13): diversity should be encouraged within correct responses, not across all outputs.

Table 3 shows that global entropy regularization provides only marginal and inconsistent gains over GRPO. The best average Pass@64 is obtained at τent=0.001\tau_{\mathrm{ent}}=0.001, improving over GRPO by only +0.19+0.19 points (82.04 vs. 81.85). The effect also varies across benchmarks: for example, τent=0.0005\tau_{\mathrm{ent}}=0.0005 improves AMC Pass@64 but substantially hurts AIME Pass@64, and no coefficient consistently improves all datasets. These results support our claim that global entropy is a brittle mechanism for improving multi-sample coverage, because it acts over the full output space rather than specifically reallocating probability within the correct set.

Appendix D Experimental Details

D.1 Datasets

We use the RL training dataset from Liao et al. [2025], derived from DeepScaleR 40k corpus [Luo et al., 2025]. The training pool consists of competition-style mathematical reasoning problems drawn from MATH [Hendrycks et al., 2021], AIME (1983–2023) problem sets, AMC (pre-2023) contests, and Omni-MATH [Gao et al., 2024], with difficulty rebalancing to reduce trivial problems and improve RL training efficiency. The final training set contains 10,000 problems, with an additional 500 problems reserved for validation.

D.2 Models

We evaluate on three models spanning different scales and pretraining approaches: DeepSeek-R1 series: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B [DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025] as well as Qwen2.5-7B [Team, 2024]. These models span both general model and distillation models, while also covering different parameter scales (1.5B to 7B). All models are initialized from publicly released checkpoints and fine-tuned using the same RLVR training pipeline.

D.3 Implementation and Evaluation Details

Hyperparameters are listed in Table  4,  5 and  6. For evaluation we report Pass@1 and Pass@K (K=64K=64) across five benchmarks. Pass@K measures the fraction of problems for which at least one of KK sampled completions is accepted by the verifier. For each benchmark problem, we sample 64 rollouts at temperature 1.0. For inference for each benchmark problem, we sample rollouts using temperature 1.01.0 and maximum generation length of 30723072 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 40964096 for Qwen-2.5-7B.

Appendix E Additional Results

E.1 Pass@K Experiments

Figures 7 present the Pass@K curves for K∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,64}K\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64\} on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen-2.5-7B, respectively, across all five benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, AMC, MATH, OlympiadBench). We compare UCPO against all baselines: GRPO, KL-Cov, Ent-Reg, Ent-Adv, Pass@K Training, and FGRPO. UCPO curves maintain improved performance through K=64K=64. The gap between UCPO and GRPO widens monotonically with KK especially across harder datasets such as AIME. On the 7B model, this gap is particularly pronounced on AIME24 (up to +10+10 points at K=64K=64).

E.2 Cost Overhead

Figure 8 shows that UCPO and GRPO have effectively identical per-step training time. UCPO’s only additional computation is the O⁡(n)O(n) scalar advantage reweighting (Eq. 52), which is negligible relative to rollout generation and the policy gradient backward pass. UCPO requires no additional forward passes, no reference model, and no extra rollouts.

E.3 Sensitivity to τ\tau

UCPO introduces a single hyperparameter τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] that interpolates between standard GRPO (τ=0\tau=0) and fully uniform-correct weighting (τ=1\tau=1). We evaluate sensitivity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B across four values: τ∈{0.2,0.3,0.4,0.5}\tau\in\{0.2,0.3,0.4,0.5\}.

Results are shown in Table 7. Several patterns emerge. First, the diversity gains (Pass@64) are robust over GRPO (τ=0\tau=0) by +1.2+1.2 to +2.7+2.7 points. Second, Pass@1 remains competitive for τ≤0.4\tau\leq 0.4. Third, at τ=0.5\tau=0.5, Pass@64 begins to degrade, particularly on AIME (56.6756.67, below GRPO). This is consistent with the theoretical expectation: at high τ\tau, the gradient is dominated by the uniform term 𝔼y∼u​[∇log⁡πθ​(y)]\mathbb{E}_{y\sim u}[\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}(y)], which may over-correct by distributing gradient signal too aggressively toward low-probability solutions, the importance weights vi=1/q^iv_{i}=1/\hat{q}_{i} become large and noisy (high variance), which can destabilize training.

These results suggest that τ\tau provides a robust operating range. The diversity–correctness trade-off is mild: Pass@64 improves substantially while Pass@1 fluctuates within normal variance. We use τ=0.2\tau=0.2 as the default throughout our experiments as it yields the strongest Pass@64 improvements.

We also evaluated global entropy regularization across different entropy coefficients (Table 3). Compared with UCPO, global entropy regularization underperforms at Pass@64 and is more sensitive to its coefficient. This shows that global entropy is a less effective mechanism for improving multi-sample coverage, consistent with its action over the full output space rather than the conditional distribution over verifier-accepted responses.

Appendix F Equation Diversity

We compute equational diversity following [Hu et al., 2025]. For each prompt, we consider only correct rollouts. From each rollout, we extract formulas appearing inside LaTeX math delimiters ($...$, \(...\), \[...\]) within the first LL characters of the response. For rollout ii, let FiF_{i} denote the set of extracted formulas.

We define the equation uniqueness score for rollout ii as

Deq(i)=|Fi∖⋃j≠iFj|max⁡(1,|Fi|).D_{\mathrm{eq}}^{(i)}=\frac{\left|F_{i}\setminus\bigcup_{j\neq i}F_{j}\right|}{\max\left(1,|F_{i}|\right)}.

This score measures the fraction of formulas in rollout ii that do not appear in any other correct rollout for the same prompt. We average Deq(i)D_{\mathrm{eq}}^{(i)} across correct rollouts to obtain a prompt-level score, and then average across prompts within each dataset. Higher values indicate greater equation-level diversity among correct solutions.
